headline: High: shared filesystem/MCP and broad egress make prompt injection, leakage, and action-conflict plausible by default.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Agent A ingests MCP/OpenAPI tools and browser content; Agent B uses MCP and browser-based workflows. B’s workspace/filesystem and A’s persistent shared sessions create a plausible bridge where attacker-controlled content from A can be parsed by B as instructions. The interaction is documented enough to exceed medium, and uncertainty favors higher severity.
conditions: IF A writes attacker-controlled text into a shared workspace or MCP payload that B later reads, prompt injection is possible.
IF B is configured to consume A-generated browser/file content as instructions, the pathway is active.
mitigations: Disable shared workspace handoff between agents.
Restrict MCP servers to allowlisted, provenance-tagged outputs.
Insert a manual review step before B consumes A-produced content.
Run A and B in separate OS users or containers.
requires-engineering: add content provenance labels to all inter-agent artifacts.

B_data_leakage.rationale: A touches prompts, chat messages, documents, notes, calendar events, files, and API keys, while B reads and writes workspace files and sends data to configured model APIs/MCP servers. Because both have broad network egress and shared-state paths, sensitive A data can flow into B outputs or third-party services by default. This is a direct leakage pathway, not just a theoretical one.
conditions: IF A stores prompts, API keys, or documents in a shared volume that B can read, leakage is possible.
IF B forwards workspace contents to a configured model API or MCP server, A-origin data can leave the boundary.
mitigations: Separate storage volumes for A and B.
Remove secrets from any shared workspace before B runs.
Disable automatic file upload/sync in B.
Use distinct API principals for each agent.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent data-loss-prevention filters.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: A can write to local files and mounted volumes and uses persistent shared sessions; B can read/write the filesystem, modify git state, and execute shell commands. Both also have broad network egress. In a shared repo or workspace, concurrent writes and git mutations can collide and corrupt state. The overlap is explicit in both profiles, so this is a high-confidence conflict risk.
conditions: IF A and B operate on the same mounted directory or repo, write conflicts can occur.
IF B commits or rebases while A is updating shared files, git state corruption is possible.
mitigations: Assign separate working directories.
Serialize writes with a lock file or queue.
Pause A while B performs git operations.
Use branch-per-agent workflows.
requires-engineering: add optimistic concurrency checks around shared artifacts.

D_cascading_error.rationale: A can generate web-sourced or tool-sourced content through browsers, search, and MCP/OpenAPI tools; B can act on workspace files and shell commands with approval. If B treats A’s output as authoritative, errors or hallucinations can cascade into code changes, commits, or external actions. Because B has downstream action authority, the blast radius is high.
conditions: IF B uses A-generated facts or citations without independent verification, cascading error is active.
IF A’s browser-derived output is copied into B’s shell or git actions, downstream harm can occur.
mitigations: Require B to verify A outputs against primary sources.
Block direct copy-through from A to B for executable actions.
Use a checklist before shell or git steps.
Limit B to read-only review mode for A outputs.
requires-engineering: add automated source-validation gates.

E_compliance.rationale: A handles API keys, calendar events, documents, and persistent memory; B handles source code and browser screenshots. Both have broad network egress, but the profiles do not specify residency or certification mismatches. The main compliance concern is retention and cross-boundary handling of sensitive A data when B reads shared files or uploads them to external services.
conditions: IF sensitive documents or API keys from A are stored in a workspace B can access, retention and disclosure obligations may be triggered.
IF B sends shared workspace contents to external model APIs, policy mismatches can arise.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of shared workspaces.
Review retention settings on both agents.
Use separate API keys and tenants.
Disable external uploads for sensitive projects.
requires-engineering: document residency and retention controls per agent.
